title: Machine learning foundations
why: LLMs are machine learning models, and interviewers expect you to know the basics underneath them: how a model learns from data, how you know it works and why it overfits. Learn the concepts, then build them; you need the intuition and the code, not the proofs.
outcomes: Explain supervised learning, features, labels and loss
Fit a model with gradient descent and explain what it did
Evaluate a classifier with precision, recall and a baseline
Describe how neural networks, embeddings and transformers connect
lessons: What machine learning is: data, features, labels and loss (StatQuest first, then Andrew Ng)
Linear regression and gradient descent, by hand then in code
Classification, train and test splits, and overfitting
Evaluating models: precision, recall, F1 and baselines
Neural networks in one page: from neurons to embeddings and transformers
The scikit-learn workflow: an end-to-end project from Hands-On Machine Learning, chapter 2
resources: Course 1 and the first half of course 2 are enough here
Watch the concept first: short, clear, no maths fear
Hands-On Machine Learning with Scikit-Learn and PyTorch
Optional; chapter 2 is the end-to-end project. Free notebooks on the author's GitHub
method: Learn the concepts, then build: watch the StatQuest video on a topic (about 15 minutes), then the matching Andrew Ng lecture, then write it in code here. Don't let the maths scare you: if you can explain it in a sentence and run it, you know enough for this job.
build: A notebook that trains a classifier on a public dataset, compares it with a simple baseline, reports precision and recall, and explains in plain English when you would trust it.

quiz.q: In supervised learning, the label is:
o: The answer the model learns to predict
quiz.e: Features go in; the label is what you predict.

o: Adjusts parameters step by step to reduce the loss
quiz.e: It follows the slope of the loss downhill.

quiz.q: Great training scores but poor test scores means:
quiz.e: The model memorised the training data.

quiz.q: On a dataset that is 95% one class, 95% accuracy:
o: Might mean the model always predicts the majority class
Of predicted positives, how many were right?
Of actual positives, how many did we find?
quiz.e: Recall is coverage of the real positives.
